Surah al-Mujadila is Madani and has twenty-two verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Allah has indeed heard the speech of her who pleads with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah. Allah hears your mutual dialogue. Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Seeing.﴾ ﴿Those of you who declare their wives unlawful as their mothers (who divorce by zihar) — their wives are not their mothers. Their mothers are only those who gave birth to them. Indeed, they utter an objectionable word and a falsehood. And indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving.﴾ ﴿And those who declare their wives unlawful by zihar and then retract what they said — the freeing of a slave before they touch each other. That is what you are admonished with. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ ﴿But whoever does not find [a slave], then fasting two consecutive months before they touch each other. But whoever is unable, then feeding sixty needy people. That is so that you may believe in Allah and His Messenger. These are the limits of Allah. And for the disbelievers is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who oppose Allah and His Messenger will be humiliated as those before them were humiliated. And We have already sent down clear signs, and for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment.﴾ ﴿On the Day when Allah will resurrect them all and inform them of what they did. Allah has enumerated it, and they have forgotten it. And Allah is Witness over all things.﴾ ﴿Have you not considered that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth? There is no private conversation of three but that He is their fourth, nor of five but that He is their sixth, nor of less than that or more but that He is with them wherever they are. Then He will inform them of what they did on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾

This surah is Madani. Al-Kalbi said: except for His words, ﴿There is no private conversation of three but that He is their fourth﴾. And from ʿAta': the first ten verses of it are Madani and the rest are Meccan.

The majority of reciters read ﴿قَدْ سَمِعَ﴾ (qad sami'a) with clear pronunciation (bayan, i.e., without assimilation of the dal into the sin). Abu ʿAmr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Muhaysin read it with idgham (assimilation of the dal into the following sin). Khalaf ibn Hisham al-Bazzar said: I heard al-Kisa'i say: "Whoever reads qad sami'a and makes the dal clear before the sin, his tongue is foreign (a'jami), not Arabic." This statement is not to be considered; the majority hold to clear pronunciation.

The woman who pleads (al-lati tujadiluka) is Khawla bint Tha'laba — it is also said in diminutive form — or Khawla bint Khuwaylid, or Khawla bint Hakim, or Khawla bint Dulayj, or Jamila, or Khawla bint al-Samit. These are the views of the early scholars (al-salaf). Most narrators hold that the husband in this incident was Aws ibn al-Samit, brother of ʿUbada. It was also said that Salama ibn Sakhr al-Bayadi made zihar against his wife. His wife said: "O Messenger of Allah, Aws consumed my youth and I bore him children, and when I grew old and my family died, he made zihar against me." He said to her: "I do not see you except that you have become unlawful to him." She said: "O Messenger of Allah, do not do so, for I am alone and have no family other than him." He returned her to the same statement, and she returned to him. This is her pleading. During that, she was saying: "O Allah, I have young children from him. If I join them to him, they are lost; and if I join them to myself, they go hungry." This is her complaint to Allah, and the revelation came down during her pleading.

ʿAisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "Glory be to Him whose hearing encompasses all voices. Some of Khawla's speech was hidden from me, but Allah heard her pleading. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent for Aws and presented to him the expiation of zihar, freeing a slave. He said: 'I do not own [one].' Then fasting. He said: 'I am not able.' Then feeding. He said: 'I find nothing except that you help me.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) helped him with fifteen sa' [of dates], and prayed for him, and he made expiation by feeding and refrained from his wife." ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, used to honour Khawla when she entered upon him and would say: "Allah has indeed heard her." Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning of qad is expectation (tawaqquʿ), because the Prophet (ﷺ) and the woman were both expecting that Allah would hear her pleading and her complaint and send down what would relieve her. End of quotation.

Al-Harameyn and Abu ʿAmr read ﴿يَظَّهَّرُونَ﴾ (yazzahharun) with doubled letters (shadda); al-Akhawan and Ibn ʿAmir read ﴿يُظاهِرُونَ﴾ (yuzahiruna), the present tense of ẓāhara. Ubayy read ﴿يَتَظاهَرُونَ﴾ (yatazahharun), the present tense of tazāhara. And from him (Ubayy, or another narrator): ﴿يَتَظَهَّرُونَ﴾ (yatazahharun), the present tense of tazahhara. The meaning of all of them is zihar, which is a man's saying to his wife: "You are to me like the back of my mother," meaning in prohibition. It seems to be an allusion to riding, since their customary usage of the back refers to the backs of animals. The meaning is that he does not mount her as he does not mount his mother. For this reason the Arabs say, in contrast to this: "I dismounted from my wife," meaning: I divorced her. His words ﴿مِنكم﴾ (minkum, "of you") point to a rebuke of the Arabs and a censure of their custom of zihar, because it was among the oaths of the people of ignorance specifically, not of other nations.

The majority read ﴿أُمَّهاتِهِمْ﴾ (ummahatihim) in the accusative (naṣb), according to the dialect of the Hijaz. Al-Mufaddal from ʿAsim read it in the nominative (raf'), according to the dialect of Tamim. Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿بِأُمَّهاتِهِمْ﴾ (bi-ummahatihim) with an added bā'. Al-Zamakhshari said: "In the dialect of those who use the accusative." End of quotation. He means that the bā' is not added in the dialect of Tamim. This is not correct, and it has been refuted against al-Zamakhshari. The addition of bā' in phrases such as ﴿ما زَيْدٌ بِقائِمٍ﴾ (ma Zaydun bi-qa'im, "Zayd is not standing") is common in the dialect of Tamim. Al-Zamakhshari followed in this Abu ʿAli al-Farisi, may Allah have mercy on him.

Since the meaning of "like my mother's back" is "like my mother in prohibition," and the particular back that belongs to the body is not intended, the negation came with the words ﴿ما هُنَّ أُمَّهاتِهِمْ﴾ (mā hunna ummahātihim, "their wives are not their mothers"). Then He affirmed this with the words ﴿إنْ أُمَّهاتُهُمْ﴾ (in ummahatuhum, "their mothers are only"), i.e., in reality, ﴿إلّا اللّائِي ولَدْنَهُمْ﴾ (illa'l-la'i waladnahum, "except those who gave birth to them"). With them in prohibition He linked the mothers of foster-suckling (ummahat al-rida') and the mothers of the believers (ummahat al-mu'minin), the wives of the Messenger (ﷺ). Wives are not mothers in reality, nor are they joined to them. So the words of the one who makes zihar are "an objectionable word" (munkaran min al-qawl), which reality rejects and which the Sacred Law rejects. "And falsehood" (zuran) means a lie, baseless and deviating from the truth. It is forbidden with the prohibition of disliked acts in the extreme. When it occurs, it obligates (expiation). Allah, Exalted, gave hope after it with His words ﴿وإنَّ اللَّهَ لَعَفُوٌّ غَفُورٌ﴾ (wa inna Allaha la-ʿafuwwun ghafur, "And indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving"), together with the expiation. Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿And indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving﴾ for what has passed from him if he repents of it and does not return to it." End of quotation. This is a Mu'tazili tendency.

The apparent view is that zihar occurs only with the mother alone. If he said, "You are to me like the back of my sister or my daughter," it would not be zihar. This is the view of Qatada, al-Sha'bi and Dawud, and a narration of Abu Thawr from al-Shafi'i. The majority — al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri, al-Awza'i, al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa, Malik, and al-Shafi'i in one view — said it is zihar. The apparent view is that the dhimmi (non-Muslim under protection) is not bound by his zihar, because of His words ﴿مِنكم﴾ ("of you"), i.e., of the believers. Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i held this, because she is not among his wives. Malik said: he is bound by his zihar if he marries her, and it is valid from a revocably divorced wife (raj'iyya). Al-Muzani said it is not valid. Some scholars said: the zihar of one who has not consummated the marriage is not valid. If he made zihar against his slave-woman whom it is lawful for him to have intercourse with, it binds him according to Malik. Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i said it does not bind him. The cause of the disagreement is: does she fall under ﴿نِسائِهِمْ﴾ (nisa'ihim, "their wives") or not? The apparent view is that the zihar of a slave (ʿabd) is valid, because he falls under ﴿يُظاهِرُونَ مِنكم﴾ ("those of you who make zihar"), since he is one of the Muslims. If freeing a slave and feeding are impossible for him, he is able to fast. Al-Tha'labi related from Malik that his zihar is not valid, and that a woman is not included among "those who make zihar." So if she made zihar against her husband, it would be nothing. Al-Hasan ibn Ziyad said: she becomes one who has made zihar. Al-Awza'i, ʿAta', Ishaq and Abu Yusuf said: if she says to her husband, "You are to me like the back of so-and-so," it is an oath which she expiates. Al-Zuhri said: "I think she should make the expiation of zihar, and her saying this does not prevent her from being with her husband in intercourse."

The apparent meaning of God's words ﴿then they go back on what they said﴾ is that they return to the same wording that was said by them, namely the man saying a second time, "You are to me like the back of my mother." Thus expiation is not incurred by the utterance itself, but only by the second one. This is the position of the Ahl al-Zahir (the Literalists, or Zahiri school). It is also reported from Bukayr ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Ashajj, Abu al-Aliyah, and Abu Hanifa, and it is the view of al-Farra'. Tawus, Qatada, al-Zuhri, al-Hasan, Malik, and a group of scholars said: ﴿what they said﴾ means "for intercourse." The meaning is: for what they said, that they would not go back to it. So if a man makes zihar (the pre-Islamic form of divorce in which a husband compares his wife to his mother's back) and then has intercourse, expiation becomes obligatory for him, even if he divorces her or she dies. Abu Hanifa, Malik as well, al-Shafi'i, and a group said: the meaning is that they go back on what they said by resolving to retain her and to have intercourse. Whenever he resolves on that, expiation becomes obligatory for him, whether he divorces her or she dies. Al-Shafi'i said: the return that makes expiation obligatory is that he withholds from divorcing her after zihar, and a period of time passes in which he could have divorced her but does not. Some said: the meaning is: "Those who make zihar from their wives in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance)", that is, zihar was their custom, and then they return to that practice in Islam. This was stated by al-Qutabi. Al-Akhfash said: there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it, and the intended sense is: ﴿then freeing a neck﴾ for what they said. This view is worthless, because it disrupts the composition of the verse.

﴿freeing a neck﴾. The apparent meaning is that any neck (any slave) suffices, so a non-believing slave is acceptable. Malik and al-Shafi'i said: Islam is a condition for it, as with the slave in expiation for killing. The apparent meaning is that a mukatab (a slave who has contracted to purchase his freedom) is acceptable, because he is still a slave as long as a single dirham remains owed. Abu Hanifa and his companions also held this. If someone frees half of two slaves, it is not sufficient, according to Abu Hanifa and his companions. Al-Shafi'i said it is sufficient.

﴿before they touch one another﴾. It is not permitted for the one who has made zihar to have intercourse until he has made expiation. If he does so, he has sinned, and the expiation is not waived from him. Mujahid said: another expiation is incurred upon him. It was also said: the expiation obligatory upon him falls away, and nothing else is incumbent on him. The hadith of Aws ibn al-Samit refutes this view. This applies whether the expiation is by freeing a slave, by fasting, or by feeding the poor. Abu Hanifa said: if the expiation is by feeding, it is permissible for him to have intercourse and then feed the poor. This is the apparent meaning of His words: ﴿but whoever cannot, then feeding sixty needy persons﴾, since He did not say in it: ﴿before they touch one another﴾, while He did attach that condition to freeing and fasting. The apparent meaning of al-tamassu ("touching") is the literal sense, so it is not permissible for them to touch one another before it, nor to lie together, nor any other forms of enjoyment. This is the view of Malik and one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i. Most scholars said it means intercourse, so it is permissible for him to enjoy his wife in other ways before making expiation. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Thawri, and it is the sound position in the school of al-Shafi'i. The pronoun in (yatamassa) refers to what the discourse has referred to, namely the one who made zihar and the wife to whom it was made.

﴿That is what you are admonished with﴾. The demonstrative refers to the freeing. That is, it is an act of admonition for you, so that you may refrain from zihar.

﴿But whoever does not find﴾: that is, a neck, nor its price, or he finds it or its price but needs that money. Abu Hanifa said: he is obliged to free a slave even if he needs the money, and he does not move on to fasting. This is the apparent meaning. Al-Shafi'i said: he moves on to fasting. The two months are by the crescent moons, even if one of them comes out short, or [they are counted] by number rather than by the crescent. So he fasts until the new moon, then one month by the crescent, then he completes the first by number. The apparent meaning is that consecutiveness is obligatory. If he breaks the fast without an excuse, he must start again, or if he breaks it with an excuse such as travel or the like. Ibn al-Musayyab, Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Amr ibn Dinar, al-Sha'bi, Malik, and al-Shafi'i in one of his two opinions said: he continues building on what he has done. Al-Nakha'i, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hakam ibn Uyayna, al-Thawri, the people of ra'y (opinion), and al-Shafi'i in one of his opinions said otherwise. The apparent meaning is that if he finds a neck after he has begun fasting, he continues fasting, and it suffices for him. This is the school of Malik and al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: he is obliged to free a slave. If he has intercourse during the course of the fast, the consecutiveness is broken and he begins again. Malik and Abu Hanifa also said this. Al-Shafi'i said: it is broken if he has intercourse during the day, but not at night.

﴿But whoever is not able﴾ to fast because of a chronic illness, or because fasting weakens him severely. This is as in the hadith of Aws, when he was asked: "Are you able to fast two consecutive months?" He replied: "By God, O Messenger of God, if I do not eat for a day and a night three times, my sight fails and I fear my eyes will go blind." (ﷺ). The apparent meaning is that feeding is unrestricted, but the custom of feeding at the time of revelation specifies it, which is what satisfies people without a fixed measure of a mudd. The school of Malik holds that it is a mudd and a third by the Prophetic mudd (ﷺ). Feeding the entire number, sixty, is obligatory according to Malik and al-Shafi'i, and this is the apparent meaning. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: if one feeds one needy person half a sa' each day until he completes the number, it suffices for him.

﴿That is so that you may believe﴾. Ibn Atiyya said: the demonstrative refers to the return and to the facilitation in the act from freeing to fasting and feeding. Then He emphasized with His words: ﴿And these are the limits of God﴾: that is, hold to them and stop at them. Then He threatened the disbelievers with this legal ruling. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is the explanation, instruction, and drawing attention to the rulings, so that you may affirm belief in God and His Messenger in acting upon the laws He has prescribed concerning zihar and other matters, and abandon what you were upon in your jahiliyyah, ﴿and these are the limits of God﴾, which may not be transgressed, and ﴿for the disbelievers﴾ who do not follow them or act upon them, ﴿is a painful punishment.﴾ End of quotation.

﴿Indeed, those who oppose God and His Messenger﴾. It was revealed concerning the polytheists of Quraysh, who were humiliated on the day of the Trench by defeat, just as those who fought the messengers before them were humiliated. When He mentioned the believers who stop at His limits, He mentioned those who oppose and differ from them. Al-muhadda means enmity and opposition concerning the limits. (kubitu): Qatada said: they were humiliated. Al-Suddi said: they were cursed. It was said: this is the dialect of Madhhij. Ibn Zayd and Abu Rawq said: they were turned back in disgrace. Al-Farra' said: they were enraged on the day of the Trench.

﴿As those before them were humiliated﴾: that is, those who fought the prophets. It was also said: on the day of Badr. Abu Ubayda and al-Akhfash said: they were destroyed. From Abu Ubayda: the ta' is a substitute for the dal, meaning kubidu: a disease struck their livers. It was said: those before them are the hypocrites of the nations. It was said: kubitu has the sense of sa-yukbatun ("they will be humiliated"), and this is good news to the believers of victory. He expressed it in the past tense to affirm that it will certainly occur. The discussion of the root kabata has already passed in Al 'Imran.

﴿And We have sent down clear signs﴾ as proof of the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the soundness of what he brought. (For the disbelievers): that is, those who oppose him, ﴿is a humiliating punishment﴾: that is, it will humiliate and abase them. The governing element of "the day He raises them" is either what governs "for the disbelievers" or "humiliating," or "mention," or the phrase is an answer to someone who asked: "When will be the punishment of these people?" So it was said to him: ﴿The day God raises them﴾: that is, it will be on the day God raises them. (Jami'an) is in the accusative as a state (hal): that is, gathered in one place, or its meaning is all of them, since jami' may bear both meanings. ﴿Then He will inform them of what they did﴾, as a rebuke and reproach to them. (Ahsahu) with all its details, its quantity, its manner, its time and its place. (Nasuhu): because of their belittling of it and their disdain that any reckoning would fall upon them for it. (Shahid): nothing is hidden from Him. The majority read ma yakunu with the ya'; Abu Ja'far, Abu Haywa, and Shayba read it with the ta', because al-najwa is feminine. Sahib al-Lawami said: if it is governed by the preposition, it is in the position of: "What came to me from a woman," except that in this construction the masculine is more common, in agreement with the common reading. He said: because it is attached to "from secret counsel," and that requires the collective, which is masculine. End of quotation. But the feminine is not more common in this construction, because min is extra. The verb is attributed to a feminine noun, so the feminine is more common, and it is the analogical form, as God says: ﴿And there does not come to them any sign from the signs of their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 4], ﴿No nation precedes its term﴾ [al-Hijr: 5]. Here the verb is complete (taamma), and najwa may be a verbal noun (masdar) added to three, that is, from the secret talk of three, or a verbal noun with an omitted modifier, that is, from those who hold secret counsel, or a verbal noun applied to the group conversing secretly, so "three" is in those two readings. Ibn Atiyya said: it is a substitute or an attribute. Al-Zamakhshari said: an attribute. Ibn Abi Ablah read thalatha and khamsa in the accusative as states, with the governing element being yatanajawna implied, indicated by najwa. Al-Zamakhshari said: or by interpreting najwa as "those conversing secretly," and its accusative is from the pronoun in it. Ibn Isa said: every secret conversation is najwa. Ibn Surraqa said: sirar is what occurs between two, and najwa is what occurs among more. It was said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, and the three and the five were singled out because the hypocrites used to converse secretly in these two numbers to enrage the people of faith. The clause after illa in the three places is in the position of a state, and His being the fourth of them, the sixth of them, and with them through knowledge and awareness of what they converse about. Ibn Abbas said: it was revealed concerning Rabi'a and Habib, the two sons of Amr, and Safwan ibn Umayya. They talked, and one of them said: "Do you think God knows what we say?" The other said: "He knows some of it and does not know some of it." The third said: "If He knows some of it, then He knows all of it."

﴿Nor less than that﴾: this refers to the three and the five. Less than three is two, and less than five is four. ﴿Nor more﴾ indicates what follows six and beyond. The majority read (wa la akthara) in conjunction with the form of the genitive; al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-A'mash, Abu Haywa, Sallam, and Ya'qub read it in the nominative, in conjunction with the position of najwa if it is meant as those conversing. Whoever makes it a pure verbal noun with an omitted modifier, meaning "nor secret conversation less," then the modifier is omitted and the modified (the pronoun) is placed in its position, and it is inflected by its inflection. It is permissible that (wa la adna) be a subject, and the predicate is ﴿except that He is with them﴾, so it is a conjunction of sentences. Al-Hasan also, Mujahid, al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, and Ya'qub also read wa la akbara with a ba' and nominative, and this admits two grammatical analyses: conjunction with the position, or nominative as a subject. It was read (yunbi'uhum) with lightening and hamza; Zayd ibn Ali read it with lightening and no hamza, with a kasra on the ha'. The majority read it with emphasis, hamza, and a damma on the ha'.

This surah is Madani. Al-Kalbi said: except for His words, ﴿There is no private conversation of three but that He is their fourth﴾. And from ʿAta': the first ten verses of it are Madani and the rest are Meccan.

The majority of reciters read ﴿قَدْ سَمِعَ﴾ (qad sami'a) with clear pronunciation (bayan, i.e., without assimilation of the dal into the sin). Abu ʿAmr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Muhaysin read it with idgham (assimilation of the dal into the following sin). Khalaf ibn Hisham al-Bazzar said: I heard al-Kisa'i say: "Whoever reads qad sami'a and makes the dal clear before the sin, his tongue is foreign (a'jami), not Arabic." This statement is not to be considered; the majority hold to clear pronunciation.

The woman who pleads (al-lati tujadiluka) is Khawla bint Tha'laba — it is also said in diminutive form — or Khawla bint Khuwaylid, or Khawla bint Hakim, or Khawla bint Dulayj, or Jamila, or Khawla bint al-Samit. These are the views of the early scholars (al-salaf). Most narrators hold that the husband in this incident was Aws ibn al-Samit, brother of ʿUbada. It was also said that Salama ibn Sakhr al-Bayadi made zihar against his wife. His wife said: "O Messenger of Allah, Aws consumed my youth and I bore him children, and when I grew old and my family died, he made zihar against me." He said to her: "I do not see you except that you have become unlawful to him." She said: "O Messenger of Allah, do not do so, for I am alone and have no family other than him." He returned her to the same statement, and she returned to him. This is her pleading. During that, she was saying: "O Allah, I have young children from him. If I join them to him, they are lost; and if I join them to myself, they go hungry." This is her complaint to Allah, and the revelation came down during her pleading.

ʿAisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "Glory be to Him whose hearing encompasses all voices. Some of Khawla's speech was hidden from me, but Allah heard her pleading. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent for Aws and presented to him the expiation of zihar, freeing a slave. He said: 'I do not own [one].' Then fasting. He said: 'I am not able.' Then feeding. He said: 'I find nothing except that you help me.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) helped him with fifteen sa' [of dates], and prayed for him, and he made expiation by feeding and refrained from his wife." ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, used to honour Khawla when she entered upon him and would say: "Allah has indeed heard her." Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning of qad is expectation (tawaqquʿ), because the Prophet (ﷺ) and the woman were both expecting that Allah would hear her pleading and her complaint and send down what would relieve her. End of quotation.

Al-Harameyn and Abu ʿAmr read ﴿يَظَّهَّرُونَ﴾ (yazzahharun) with doubled letters (shadda); al-Akhawan and Ibn ʿAmir read ﴿يُظاهِرُونَ﴾ (yuzahiruna), the present tense of ẓāhara. Ubayy read ﴿يَتَظاهَرُونَ﴾ (yatazahharun), the present tense of tazāhara. And from him (Ubayy, or another narrator): ﴿يَتَظَهَّرُونَ﴾ (yatazahharun), the present tense of tazahhara. The meaning of all of them is zihar, which is a man's saying to his wife: "You are to me like the back of my mother," meaning in prohibition. It seems to be an allusion to riding, since their customary usage of the back refers to the backs of animals. The meaning is that he does not mount her as he does not mount his mother. For this reason the Arabs say, in contrast to this: "I dismounted from my wife," meaning: I divorced her. His words ﴿مِنكم﴾ (minkum, "of you") point to a rebuke of the Arabs and a censure of their custom of zihar, because it was among the oaths of the people of ignorance specifically, not of other nations.

The majority read ﴿أُمَّهاتِهِمْ﴾ (ummahatihim) in the accusative (naṣb), according to the dialect of the Hijaz. Al-Mufaddal from ʿAsim read it in the nominative (raf'), according to the dialect of Tamim. Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿بِأُمَّهاتِهِمْ﴾ (bi-ummahatihim) with an added bā'. Al-Zamakhshari said: "In the dialect of those who use the accusative." End of quotation. He means that the bā' is not added in the dialect of Tamim. This is not correct, and it has been refuted against al-Zamakhshari. The addition of bā' in phrases such as ﴿ما زَيْدٌ بِقائِمٍ﴾ (ma Zaydun bi-qa'im, "Zayd is not standing") is common in the dialect of Tamim. Al-Zamakhshari followed in this Abu ʿAli al-Farisi, may Allah have mercy on him.

Since the meaning of "like my mother's back" is "like my mother in prohibition," and the particular back that belongs to the body is not intended, the negation came with the words ﴿ما هُنَّ أُمَّهاتِهِمْ﴾ (mā hunna ummahātihim, "their wives are not their mothers"). Then He affirmed this with the words ﴿إنْ أُمَّهاتُهُمْ﴾ (in ummahatuhum, "their mothers are only"), i.e., in reality, ﴿إلّا اللّائِي ولَدْنَهُمْ﴾ (illa'l-la'i waladnahum, "except those who gave birth to them"). With them in prohibition He linked the mothers of foster-suckling (ummahat al-rida') and the mothers of the believers (ummahat al-mu'minin), the wives of the Messenger (ﷺ). Wives are not mothers in reality, nor are they joined to them. So the words of the one who makes zihar are "an objectionable word" (munkaran min al-qawl), which reality rejects and which the Sacred Law rejects. "And falsehood" (zuran) means a lie, baseless and deviating from the truth. It is forbidden with the prohibition of disliked acts in the extreme. When it occurs, it obligates (expiation). Allah, Exalted, gave hope after it with His words ﴿وإنَّ اللَّهَ لَعَفُوٌّ غَفُورٌ﴾ (wa inna Allaha la-ʿafuwwun ghafur, "And indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving"), together with the expiation. Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿And indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving﴾ for what has passed from him if he repents of it and does not return to it." End of quotation. This is a Mu'tazili tendency.

The apparent view is that zihar occurs only with the mother alone. If he said, "You are to me like the back of my sister or my daughter," it would not be zihar. This is the view of Qatada, al-Sha'bi and Dawud, and a narration of Abu Thawr from al-Shafi'i. The majority — al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri, al-Awza'i, al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa, Malik, and al-Shafi'i in one view — said it is zihar. The apparent view is that the dhimmi (non-Muslim under protection) is not bound by his zihar, because of His words ﴿مِنكم﴾ ("of you"), i.e., of the believers. Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i held this, because she is not among his wives. Malik said: he is bound by his zihar if he marries her, and it is valid from a revocably divorced wife (raj'iyya). Al-Muzani said it is not valid. Some scholars said: the zihar of one who has not consummated the marriage is not valid. If he made zihar against his slave-woman whom it is lawful for him to have intercourse with, it binds him according to Malik. Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i said it does not bind him. The cause of the disagreement is: does she fall under ﴿نِسائِهِمْ﴾ (nisa'ihim, "their wives") or not? The apparent view is that the zihar of a slave (ʿabd) is valid, because he falls under ﴿يُظاهِرُونَ مِنكم﴾ ("those of you who make zihar"), since he is one of the Muslims. If freeing a slave and feeding are impossible for him, he is able to fast. Al-Tha'labi related from Malik that his zihar is not valid, and that a woman is not included among "those who make zihar." So if she made zihar against her husband, it would be nothing. Al-Hasan ibn Ziyad said: she becomes one who has made zihar. Al-Awza'i, ʿAta', Ishaq and Abu Yusuf said: if she says to her husband, "You are to me like the back of so-and-so," it is an oath which she expiates. Al-Zuhri said: "I think she should make the expiation of zihar, and her saying this does not prevent her from being with her husband in intercourse."

The apparent meaning of God's words ﴿then they go back on what they said﴾ is that they return to the same wording that was said by them, namely the man saying a second time, "You are to me like the back of my mother." Thus expiation is not incurred by the utterance itself, but only by the second one. This is the position of the Ahl al-Zahir (the Literalists, or Zahiri school). It is also reported from Bukayr ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Ashajj, Abu al-Aliyah, and Abu Hanifa, and it is the view of al-Farra'. Tawus, Qatada, al-Zuhri, al-Hasan, Malik, and a group of scholars said: ﴿what they said﴾ means "for intercourse." The meaning is: for what they said, that they would not go back to it. So if a man makes zihar (the pre-Islamic form of divorce in which a husband compares his wife to his mother's back) and then has intercourse, expiation becomes obligatory for him, even if he divorces her or she dies. Abu Hanifa, Malik as well, al-Shafi'i, and a group said: the meaning is that they go back on what they said by resolving to retain her and to have intercourse. Whenever he resolves on that, expiation becomes obligatory for him, whether he divorces her or she dies. Al-Shafi'i said: the return that makes expiation obligatory is that he withholds from divorcing her after zihar, and a period of time passes in which he could have divorced her but does not. Some said: the meaning is: "Those who make zihar from their wives in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance)", that is, zihar was their custom, and then they return to that practice in Islam. This was stated by al-Qutabi. Al-Akhfash said: there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it, and the intended sense is: ﴿then freeing a neck﴾ for what they said. This view is worthless, because it disrupts the composition of the verse.

﴿freeing a neck﴾. The apparent meaning is that any neck (any slave) suffices, so a non-believing slave is acceptable. Malik and al-Shafi'i said: Islam is a condition for it, as with the slave in expiation for killing. The apparent meaning is that a mukatab (a slave who has contracted to purchase his freedom) is acceptable, because he is still a slave as long as a single dirham remains owed. Abu Hanifa and his companions also held this. If someone frees half of two slaves, it is not sufficient, according to Abu Hanifa and his companions. Al-Shafi'i said it is sufficient.

﴿before they touch one another﴾. It is not permitted for the one who has made zihar to have intercourse until he has made expiation. If he does so, he has sinned, and the expiation is not waived from him. Mujahid said: another expiation is incurred upon him. It was also said: the expiation obligatory upon him falls away, and nothing else is incumbent on him. The hadith of Aws ibn al-Samit refutes this view. This applies whether the expiation is by freeing a slave, by fasting, or by feeding the poor. Abu Hanifa said: if the expiation is by feeding, it is permissible for him to have intercourse and then feed the poor. This is the apparent meaning of His words: ﴿but whoever cannot, then feeding sixty needy persons﴾, since He did not say in it: ﴿before they touch one another﴾, while He did attach that condition to freeing and fasting. The apparent meaning of al-tamassu ("touching") is the literal sense, so it is not permissible for them to touch one another before it, nor to lie together, nor any other forms of enjoyment. This is the view of Malik and one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i. Most scholars said it means intercourse, so it is permissible for him to enjoy his wife in other ways before making expiation. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Thawri, and it is the sound position in the school of al-Shafi'i. The pronoun in (yatamassa) refers to what the discourse has referred to, namely the one who made zihar and the wife to whom it was made.

﴿That is what you are admonished with﴾. The demonstrative refers to the freeing. That is, it is an act of admonition for you, so that you may refrain from zihar.

﴿But whoever does not find﴾: that is, a neck, nor its price, or he finds it or its price but needs that money. Abu Hanifa said: he is obliged to free a slave even if he needs the money, and he does not move on to fasting. This is the apparent meaning. Al-Shafi'i said: he moves on to fasting. The two months are by the crescent moons, even if one of them comes out short, or [they are counted] by number rather than by the crescent. So he fasts until the new moon, then one month by the crescent, then he completes the first by number. The apparent meaning is that consecutiveness is obligatory. If he breaks the fast without an excuse, he must start again, or if he breaks it with an excuse such as travel or the like. Ibn al-Musayyab, Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Amr ibn Dinar, al-Sha'bi, Malik, and al-Shafi'i in one of his two opinions said: he continues building on what he has done. Al-Nakha'i, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hakam ibn Uyayna, al-Thawri, the people of ra'y (opinion), and al-Shafi'i in one of his opinions said otherwise. The apparent meaning is that if he finds a neck after he has begun fasting, he continues fasting, and it suffices for him. This is the school of Malik and al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: he is obliged to free a slave. If he has intercourse during the course of the fast, the consecutiveness is broken and he begins again. Malik and Abu Hanifa also said this. Al-Shafi'i said: it is broken if he has intercourse during the day, but not at night.

﴿But whoever is not able﴾ to fast because of a chronic illness, or because fasting weakens him severely. This is as in the hadith of Aws, when he was asked: "Are you able to fast two consecutive months?" He replied: "By God, O Messenger of God, if I do not eat for a day and a night three times, my sight fails and I fear my eyes will go blind." (ﷺ). The apparent meaning is that feeding is unrestricted, but the custom of feeding at the time of revelation specifies it, which is what satisfies people without a fixed measure of a mudd. The school of Malik holds that it is a mudd and a third by the Prophetic mudd (ﷺ). Feeding the entire number, sixty, is obligatory according to Malik and al-Shafi'i, and this is the apparent meaning. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: if one feeds one needy person half a sa' each day until he completes the number, it suffices for him.

﴿That is so that you may believe﴾. Ibn Atiyya said: the demonstrative refers to the return and to the facilitation in the act from freeing to fasting and feeding. Then He emphasized with His words: ﴿And these are the limits of God﴾: that is, hold to them and stop at them. Then He threatened the disbelievers with this legal ruling. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is the explanation, instruction, and drawing attention to the rulings, so that you may affirm belief in God and His Messenger in acting upon the laws He has prescribed concerning zihar and other matters, and abandon what you were upon in your jahiliyyah, ﴿and these are the limits of God﴾, which may not be transgressed, and ﴿for the disbelievers﴾ who do not follow them or act upon them, ﴿is a painful punishment.﴾ End of quotation.

﴿Indeed, those who oppose God and His Messenger﴾. It was revealed concerning the polytheists of Quraysh, who were humiliated on the day of the Trench by defeat, just as those who fought the messengers before them were humiliated. When He mentioned the believers who stop at His limits, He mentioned those who oppose and differ from them. Al-muhadda means enmity and opposition concerning the limits. (kubitu): Qatada said: they were humiliated. Al-Suddi said: they were cursed. It was said: this is the dialect of Madhhij. Ibn Zayd and Abu Rawq said: they were turned back in disgrace. Al-Farra' said: they were enraged on the day of the Trench.

﴿As those before them were humiliated﴾: that is, those who fought the prophets. It was also said: on the day of Badr. Abu Ubayda and al-Akhfash said: they were destroyed. From Abu Ubayda: the ta' is a substitute for the dal, meaning kubidu: a disease struck their livers. It was said: those before them are the hypocrites of the nations. It was said: kubitu has the sense of sa-yukbatun ("they will be humiliated"), and this is good news to the believers of victory. He expressed it in the past tense to affirm that it will certainly occur. The discussion of the root kabata has already passed in Al 'Imran.

﴿And We have sent down clear signs﴾ as proof of the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the soundness of what he brought. (For the disbelievers): that is, those who oppose him, ﴿is a humiliating punishment﴾: that is, it will humiliate and abase them. The governing element of "the day He raises them" is either what governs "for the disbelievers" or "humiliating," or "mention," or the phrase is an answer to someone who asked: "When will be the punishment of these people?" So it was said to him: ﴿The day God raises them﴾: that is, it will be on the day God raises them. (Jami'an) is in the accusative as a state (hal): that is, gathered in one place, or its meaning is all of them, since jami' may bear both meanings. ﴿Then He will inform them of what they did﴾, as a rebuke and reproach to them. (Ahsahu) with all its details, its quantity, its manner, its time and its place. (Nasuhu): because of their belittling of it and their disdain that any reckoning would fall upon them for it. (Shahid): nothing is hidden from Him. The majority read ma yakunu with the ya'; Abu Ja'far, Abu Haywa, and Shayba read it with the ta', because al-najwa is feminine. Sahib al-Lawami said: if it is governed by the preposition, it is in the position of: "What came to me from a woman," except that in this construction the masculine is more common, in agreement with the common reading. He said: because it is attached to "from secret counsel," and that requires the collective, which is masculine. End of quotation. But the feminine is not more common in this construction, because min is extra. The verb is attributed to a feminine noun, so the feminine is more common, and it is the analogical form, as God says: ﴿And there does not come to them any sign from the signs of their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 4], ﴿No nation precedes its term﴾ [al-Hijr: 5]. Here the verb is complete (taamma), and najwa may be a verbal noun (masdar) added to three, that is, from the secret talk of three, or a verbal noun with an omitted modifier, that is, from those who hold secret counsel, or a verbal noun applied to the group conversing secretly, so "three" is in those two readings. Ibn Atiyya said: it is a substitute or an attribute. Al-Zamakhshari said: an attribute. Ibn Abi Ablah read thalatha and khamsa in the accusative as states, with the governing element being yatanajawna implied, indicated by najwa. Al-Zamakhshari said: or by interpreting najwa as "those conversing secretly," and its accusative is from the pronoun in it. Ibn Isa said: every secret conversation is najwa. Ibn Surraqa said: sirar is what occurs between two, and najwa is what occurs among more. It was said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, and the three and the five were singled out because the hypocrites used to converse secretly in these two numbers to enrage the people of faith. The clause after illa in the three places is in the position of a state, and His being the fourth of them, the sixth of them, and with them through knowledge and awareness of what they converse about. Ibn Abbas said: it was revealed concerning Rabi'a and Habib, the two sons of Amr, and Safwan ibn Umayya. They talked, and one of them said: "Do you think God knows what we say?" The other said: "He knows some of it and does not know some of it." The third said: "If He knows some of it, then He knows all of it."

﴿Nor less than that﴾: this refers to the three and the five. Less than three is two, and less than five is four. ﴿Nor more﴾ indicates what follows six and beyond. The majority read (wa la akthara) in conjunction with the form of the genitive; al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-A'mash, Abu Haywa, Sallam, and Ya'qub read it in the nominative, in conjunction with the position of najwa if it is meant as those conversing. Whoever makes it a pure verbal noun with an omitted modifier, meaning "nor secret conversation less," then the modifier is omitted and the modified (the pronoun) is placed in its position, and it is inflected by its inflection. It is permissible that (wa la adna) be a subject, and the predicate is ﴿except that He is with them﴾, so it is a conjunction of sentences. Al-Hasan also, Mujahid, al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, and Ya'qub also read wa la akbara with a ba' and nominative, and this admits two grammatical analyses: conjunction with the position, or nominative as a subject. It was read (yunbi'uhum) with lightening and hamza; Zayd ibn Ali read it with lightening and no hamza, with a kasra on the ha'. The majority read it with emphasis, hamza, and a damma on the ha'.

[p. 230]

Surah al-Mujadila is Madani and has twenty-two verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Allah has indeed heard the speech of her who pleads with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah. Allah hears your mutual dialogue. Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Seeing.﴾ ﴿Those of you who declare their wives unlawful as their mothers (who divorce by zihar) — their wives are not their mothers. Their mothers are only those who gave birth to them. Indeed, they utter an objectionable word and a falsehood. And indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving.﴾ ﴿And those who declare their wives unlawful by zihar and then retract what they said — the freeing of a slave before they touch each other. That is what you are admonished with. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ ﴿But whoever does not find [a slave], then fasting two consecutive months before they touch each other. But whoever is unable, then feeding sixty needy people. That is so that you may believe in Allah and His Messenger. These are the limits of Allah. And for the disbelievers is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who oppose Allah and His Messenger will be humiliated as those before them were humiliated. And We have already sent down clear signs, and for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment.﴾ ﴿On the Day when Allah will resurrect them all and inform them of what they did. Allah has enumerated it, and they have forgotten it. And Allah is Witness over all things.﴾ ﴿Have you not considered that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth? There is no private conversation of three but that He is their fourth, nor of five but that He is their sixth, nor of less than that or more but that He is with them wherever they are. Then He will inform them of what they did on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾

[p. 231]

[p. 232]

This surah is Madani. Al-Kalbi said: except for His words, ﴿There is no private conversation of three but that He is their fourth﴾. And from ʿAta': the first ten verses of it are Madani and the rest are Meccan.

The majority of reciters read ﴿قَدْ سَمِعَ﴾ (qad sami'a) with clear pronunciation (bayan, i.e., without assimilation of the dal into the sin). Abu ʿAmr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Muhaysin read it with idgham (assimilation of the dal into the following sin). Khalaf ibn Hisham al-Bazzar said: I heard al-Kisa'i say: "Whoever reads qad sami'a and makes the dal clear before the sin, his tongue is foreign (a'jami), not Arabic." This statement is not to be considered; the majority hold to clear pronunciation.

The woman who pleads (al-lati tujadiluka) is Khawla bint Tha'laba — it is also said in diminutive form — or Khawla bint Khuwaylid, or Khawla bint Hakim, or Khawla bint Dulayj, or Jamila, or Khawla bint al-Samit. These are the views of the early scholars (al-salaf). Most narrators hold that the husband in this incident was Aws ibn al-Samit, brother of ʿUbada. It was also said that Salama ibn Sakhr al-Bayadi made zihar against his wife. His wife said: "O Messenger of Allah, Aws consumed my youth and I bore him children, and when I grew old and my family died, he made zihar against me." He said to her: "I do not see you except that you have become unlawful to him." She said: "O Messenger of Allah, do not do so, for I am alone and have no family other than him." He returned her to the same statement, and she returned to him. This is her pleading. During that, she was saying: "O Allah, I have young children from him. If I join them to him, they are lost; and if I join them to myself, they go hungry." This is her complaint to Allah, and the revelation came down during her pleading.

ʿAisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "Glory be to Him whose hearing encompasses all voices. Some of Khawla's speech was hidden from me, but Allah heard her pleading. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent for Aws and presented to him the expiation of zihar, freeing a slave. He said: 'I do not own [one].' Then fasting. He said: 'I am not able.' Then feeding. He said: 'I find nothing except that you help me.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) helped him with fifteen sa' [of dates], and prayed for him, and he made expiation by feeding and refrained from his wife." ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, used to honour Khawla when she entered upon him and would say: "Allah has indeed heard her." Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning of qad is expectation (tawaqquʿ), because the Prophet (ﷺ) and the woman were both expecting that Allah would hear her pleading and her complaint and send down what would relieve her. End of quotation.

Al-Harameyn and Abu ʿAmr read ﴿يَظَّهَّرُونَ﴾ (yazzahharun) with doubled letters (shadda); al-Akhawan and Ibn ʿAmir read ﴿يُظاهِرُونَ﴾ (yuzahiruna), the present tense of ẓāhara. Ubayy read ﴿يَتَظاهَرُونَ﴾ (yatazahharun), the present tense of tazāhara. And from him (Ubayy, or another narrator): ﴿يَتَظَهَّرُونَ﴾ (yatazahharun), the present tense of tazahhara. The meaning of all of them is zihar, which is a man's saying to his wife: "You are to me like the back of my mother," meaning in prohibition. It seems to be an allusion to riding, since their customary usage of the back refers to the backs of animals. The meaning is that he does not mount her as he does not mount his mother. For this reason the Arabs say, in contrast to this: "I dismounted from my wife," meaning: I divorced her. His words ﴿مِنكم﴾ (minkum, "of you") point to a rebuke of the Arabs and a censure of their custom of zihar, because it was among the oaths of the people of ignorance specifically, not of other nations.

The majority read ﴿أُمَّهاتِهِمْ﴾ (ummahatihim) in the accusative (naṣb), according to the dialect of the Hijaz. Al-Mufaddal from ʿAsim read it in the nominative (raf'), according to the dialect of Tamim. Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿بِأُمَّهاتِهِمْ﴾ (bi-ummahatihim) with an added bā'. Al-Zamakhshari said: "In the dialect of those who use the accusative." End of quotation. He means that the bā' is not added in the dialect of Tamim. This is not correct, and it has been refuted against al-Zamakhshari. The addition of bā' in phrases such as ﴿ما زَيْدٌ بِقائِمٍ﴾ (ma Zaydun bi-qa'im, "Zayd is not standing") is common in the dialect of Tamim. Al-Zamakhshari followed in this Abu ʿAli al-Farisi, may Allah have mercy on him.

Since the meaning of "like my mother's back" is "like my mother in prohibition," and the particular back that belongs to the body is not intended, the negation came with the words ﴿ما هُنَّ أُمَّهاتِهِمْ﴾ (mā hunna ummahātihim, "their wives are not their mothers"). Then He affirmed this with the words ﴿إنْ أُمَّهاتُهُمْ﴾ (in ummahatuhum, "their mothers are only"), i.e., in reality, ﴿إلّا اللّائِي ولَدْنَهُمْ﴾ (illa'l-la'i waladnahum, "except those who gave birth to them"). With them in prohibition He linked the mothers of foster-suckling (ummahat al-rida') and the mothers of the believers (ummahat al-mu'minin), the wives of the Messenger (ﷺ). Wives are not mothers in reality, nor are they joined to them. So the words of the one who makes zihar are "an objectionable word" (munkaran min al-qawl), which reality rejects and which the Sacred Law rejects. "And falsehood" (zuran) means a lie, baseless and deviating from the truth. It is forbidden with the prohibition of disliked acts in the extreme. When it occurs, it obligates (expiation). Allah, Exalted, gave hope after it with His words ﴿وإنَّ اللَّهَ لَعَفُوٌّ غَفُورٌ﴾ (wa inna Allaha la-ʿafuwwun ghafur, "And indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving"), together with the expiation. Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿And indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving﴾ for what has passed from him if he repents of it and does not return to it." End of quotation. This is a Mu'tazili tendency.

The apparent view is that zihar occurs only with the mother alone. If he said, "You are to me like the back of my sister or my daughter," it would not be zihar. This is the view of Qatada, al-Sha'bi and Dawud, and a narration of Abu Thawr from al-Shafi'i. The majority — al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri, al-Awza'i, al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa, Malik, and al-Shafi'i in one view — said it is zihar. The apparent view is that the dhimmi (non-Muslim under protection) is not bound by his zihar, because of His words ﴿مِنكم﴾ ("of you"), i.e., of the believers. Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i held this, because she is not among his wives. Malik said: he is bound by his zihar if he marries her, and it is valid from a revocably divorced wife (raj'iyya). Al-Muzani said it is not valid. Some scholars said: the zihar of one who has not consummated the marriage is not valid. If he made zihar against his slave-woman whom it is lawful for him to have intercourse with, it binds him according to Malik. Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i said it does not bind him. The cause of the disagreement is: does she fall under ﴿نِسائِهِمْ﴾ (nisa'ihim, "their wives") or not? The apparent view is that the zihar of a slave (ʿabd) is valid, because he falls under ﴿يُظاهِرُونَ مِنكم﴾ ("those of you who make zihar"), since he is one of the Muslims. If freeing a slave and feeding are impossible for him, he is able to fast. Al-Tha'labi related from Malik that his zihar is not valid, and that a woman is not included among "those who make zihar." So if she made zihar against her husband, it would be nothing. Al-Hasan ibn Ziyad said: she becomes one who has made zihar. Al-Awza'i, ʿAta', Ishaq and Abu Yusuf said: if she says to her husband, "You are to me like the back of so-and-so," it is an oath which she expiates. Al-Zuhri said: "I think she should make the expiation of zihar, and her saying this does not prevent her from being with her husband in intercourse."

The apparent meaning of God's words ﴿then they go back on what they said﴾ is that they return to the same wording that was said by them, namely the man saying a second time, "You are to me like the back of my mother." Thus expiation is not incurred by the utterance itself, but only by the second one. This is the position of the Ahl al-Zahir (the Literalists, or Zahiri school). It is also reported from Bukayr ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Ashajj, Abu al-Aliyah, and Abu Hanifa, and it is the view of al-Farra'. Tawus, Qatada, al-Zuhri, al-Hasan, Malik, and a group of scholars said: ﴿what they said﴾ means "for intercourse." The meaning is: for what they said, that they would not go back to it. So if a man makes zihar (the pre-Islamic form of divorce in which a husband compares his wife to his mother's back) and then has intercourse, expiation becomes obligatory for him, even if he divorces her or she dies. Abu Hanifa, Malik as well, al-Shafi'i, and a group said: the meaning is that they go back on what they said by resolving to retain her and to have intercourse. Whenever he resolves on that, expiation becomes obligatory for him, whether he divorces her or she dies. Al-Shafi'i said: the return that makes expiation obligatory is that he withholds from divorcing her after zihar, and a period of time passes in which he could have divorced her but does not. Some said: the meaning is: "Those who make zihar from their wives in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance)", that is, zihar was their custom, and then they return to that practice in Islam. This was stated by al-Qutabi. Al-Akhfash said: there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it, and the intended sense is: ﴿then freeing a neck﴾ for what they said. This view is worthless, because it disrupts the composition of the verse.

﴿freeing a neck﴾. The apparent meaning is that any neck (any slave) suffices, so a non-believing slave is acceptable. Malik and al-Shafi'i said: Islam is a condition for it, as with the slave in expiation for killing. The apparent meaning is that a mukatab (a slave who has contracted to purchase his freedom) is acceptable, because he is still a slave as long as a single dirham remains owed. Abu Hanifa and his companions also held this. If someone frees half of two slaves, it is not sufficient, according to Abu Hanifa and his companions. Al-Shafi'i said it is sufficient.

﴿before they touch one another﴾. It is not permitted for the one who has made zihar to have intercourse until he has made expiation. If he does so, he has sinned, and the expiation is not waived from him. Mujahid said: another expiation is incurred upon him. It was also said: the expiation obligatory upon him falls away, and nothing else is incumbent on him. The hadith of Aws ibn al-Samit refutes this view. This applies whether the expiation is by freeing a slave, by fasting, or by feeding the poor. Abu Hanifa said: if the expiation is by feeding, it is permissible for him to have intercourse and then feed the poor. This is the apparent meaning of His words: ﴿but whoever cannot, then feeding sixty needy persons﴾, since He did not say in it: ﴿before they touch one another﴾, while He did attach that condition to freeing and fasting. The apparent meaning of al-tamassu ("touching") is the literal sense, so it is not permissible for them to touch one another before it, nor to lie together, nor any other forms of enjoyment. This is the view of Malik and one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i. Most scholars said it means intercourse, so it is permissible for him to enjoy his wife in other ways before making expiation. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Thawri, and it is the sound position in the school of al-Shafi'i. The pronoun in (yatamassa) refers to what the discourse has referred to, namely the one who made zihar and the wife to whom it was made.

﴿That is what you are admonished with﴾. The demonstrative refers to the freeing. That is, it is an act of admonition for you, so that you may refrain from zihar.

﴿But whoever does not find﴾: that is, a neck, nor its price, or he finds it or its price but needs that money. Abu Hanifa said: he is obliged to free a slave even if he needs the money, and he does not move on to fasting. This is the apparent meaning. Al-Shafi'i said: he moves on to fasting. The two months are by the crescent moons, even if one of them comes out short, or [they are counted] by number rather than by the crescent. So he fasts until the new moon, then one month by the crescent, then he completes the first by number. The apparent meaning is that consecutiveness is obligatory. If he breaks the fast without an excuse, he must start again, or if he breaks it with an excuse such as travel or the like. Ibn al-Musayyab, Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Amr ibn Dinar, al-Sha'bi, Malik, and al-Shafi'i in one of his two opinions said: he continues building on what he has done. Al-Nakha'i, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hakam ibn Uyayna, al-Thawri, the people of ra'y (opinion), and al-Shafi'i in one of his opinions said otherwise. The apparent meaning is that if he finds a neck after he has begun fasting, he continues fasting, and it suffices for him. This is the school of Malik and al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: he is obliged to free a slave. If he has intercourse during the course of the fast, the consecutiveness is broken and he begins again. Malik and Abu Hanifa also said this. Al-Shafi'i said: it is broken if he has intercourse during the day, but not at night.

﴿But whoever is not able﴾ to fast because of a chronic illness, or because fasting weakens him severely. This is as in the hadith of Aws, when he was asked: "Are you able to fast two consecutive months?" He replied: "By God, O Messenger of God, if I do not eat for a day and a night three times, my sight fails and I fear my eyes will go blind." (ﷺ). The apparent meaning is that feeding is unrestricted, but the custom of feeding at the time of revelation specifies it, which is what satisfies people without a fixed measure of a mudd. The school of Malik holds that it is a mudd and a third by the Prophetic mudd (ﷺ). Feeding the entire number, sixty, is obligatory according to Malik and al-Shafi'i, and this is the apparent meaning. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: if one feeds one needy person half a sa' each day until he completes the number, it suffices for him.

﴿That is so that you may believe﴾. Ibn Atiyya said: the demonstrative refers to the return and to the facilitation in the act from freeing to fasting and feeding. Then He emphasized with His words: ﴿And these are the limits of God﴾: that is, hold to them and stop at them. Then He threatened the disbelievers with this legal ruling. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is the explanation, instruction, and drawing attention to the rulings, so that you may affirm belief in God and His Messenger in acting upon the laws He has prescribed concerning zihar and other matters, and abandon what you were upon in your jahiliyyah, ﴿and these are the limits of God﴾, which may not be transgressed, and ﴿for the disbelievers﴾ who do not follow them or act upon them, ﴿is a painful punishment.﴾ End of quotation.

﴿Indeed, those who oppose God and His Messenger﴾. It was revealed concerning the polytheists of Quraysh, who were humiliated on the day of the Trench by defeat, just as those who fought the messengers before them were humiliated. When He mentioned the believers who stop at His limits, He mentioned those who oppose and differ from them. Al-muhadda means enmity and opposition concerning the limits. (kubitu): Qatada said: they were humiliated. Al-Suddi said: they were cursed. It was said: this is the dialect of Madhhij. Ibn Zayd and Abu Rawq said: they were turned back in disgrace. Al-Farra' said: they were enraged on the day of the Trench.

﴿As those before them were humiliated﴾: that is, those who fought the prophets. It was also said: on the day of Badr. Abu Ubayda and al-Akhfash said: they were destroyed. From Abu Ubayda: the ta' is a substitute for the dal, meaning kubidu: a disease struck their livers. It was said: those before them are the hypocrites of the nations. It was said: kubitu has the sense of sa-yukbatun ("they will be humiliated"), and this is good news to the believers of victory. He expressed it in the past tense to affirm that it will certainly occur. The discussion of the root kabata has already passed in Al 'Imran.

﴿And We have sent down clear signs﴾ as proof of the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the soundness of what he brought. (For the disbelievers): that is, those who oppose him, ﴿is a humiliating punishment﴾: that is, it will humiliate and abase them. The governing element of "the day He raises them" is either what governs "for the disbelievers" or "humiliating," or "mention," or the phrase is an answer to someone who asked: "When will be the punishment of these people?" So it was said to him: ﴿The day God raises them﴾: that is, it will be on the day God raises them. (Jami'an) is in the accusative as a state (hal): that is, gathered in one place, or its meaning is all of them, since jami' may bear both meanings. ﴿Then He will inform them of what they did﴾, as a rebuke and reproach to them. (Ahsahu) with all its details, its quantity, its manner, its time and its place. (Nasuhu): because of their belittling of it and their disdain that any reckoning would fall upon them for it. (Shahid): nothing is hidden from Him. The majority read ma yakunu with the ya'; Abu Ja'far, Abu Haywa, and Shayba read it with the ta', because al-najwa is feminine. Sahib al-Lawami said: if it is governed by the preposition, it is in the position of: "What came to me from a woman," except that in this construction the masculine is more common, in agreement with the common reading. He said: because it is attached to "from secret counsel," and that requires the collective, which is masculine. End of quotation. But the feminine is not more common in this construction, because min is extra. The verb is attributed to a feminine noun, so the feminine is more common, and it is the analogical form, as God says: ﴿And there does not come to them any sign from the signs of their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 4], ﴿No nation precedes its term﴾ [al-Hijr: 5]. Here the verb is complete (taamma), and najwa may be a verbal noun (masdar) added to three, that is, from the secret talk of three, or a verbal noun with an omitted modifier, that is, from those who hold secret counsel, or a verbal noun applied to the group conversing secretly, so "three" is in those two readings. Ibn Atiyya said: it is a substitute or an attribute. Al-Zamakhshari said: an attribute. Ibn Abi Ablah read thalatha and khamsa in the accusative as states, with the governing element being yatanajawna implied, indicated by najwa. Al-Zamakhshari said: or by interpreting najwa as "those conversing secretly," and its accusative is from the pronoun in it. Ibn Isa said: every secret conversation is najwa. Ibn Surraqa said: sirar is what occurs between two, and najwa is what occurs among more. It was said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, and the three and the five were singled out because the hypocrites used to converse secretly in these two numbers to enrage the people of faith. The clause after illa in the three places is in the position of a state, and His being the fourth of them, the sixth of them, and with them through knowledge and awareness of what they converse about. Ibn Abbas said: it was revealed concerning Rabi'a and Habib, the two sons of Amr, and Safwan ibn Umayya. They talked, and one of them said: "Do you think God knows what we say?" The other said: "He knows some of it and does not know some of it." The third said: "If He knows some of it, then He knows all of it."

﴿Nor less than that﴾: this refers to the three and the five. Less than three is two, and less than five is four. ﴿Nor more﴾ indicates what follows six and beyond. The majority read (wa la akthara) in conjunction with the form of the genitive; al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-A'mash, Abu Haywa, Sallam, and Ya'qub read it in the nominative, in conjunction with the position of najwa if it is meant as those conversing. Whoever makes it a pure verbal noun with an omitted modifier, meaning "nor secret conversation less," then the modifier is omitted and the modified (the pronoun) is placed in its position, and it is inflected by its inflection. It is permissible that (wa la adna) be a subject, and the predicate is ﴿except that He is with them﴾, so it is a conjunction of sentences. Al-Hasan also, Mujahid, al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, and Ya'qub also read wa la akbara with a ba' and nominative, and this admits two grammatical analyses: conjunction with the position, or nominative as a subject. It was read (yunbi'uhum) with lightening and hamza; Zayd ibn Ali read it with lightening and no hamza, with a kasra on the ha'. The majority read it with emphasis, hamza, and a damma on the ha'.

[p. 230]

Surah al-Mujadila is Madani and has twenty-two verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Allah has indeed heard the speech of her who pleads with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah. Allah hears your mutual dialogue. Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Seeing.﴾ ﴿Those of you who declare their wives unlawful as their mothers (who divorce by zihar) — their wives are not their mothers. Their mothers are only those who gave birth to them. Indeed, they utter an objectionable word and a falsehood. And indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving.﴾ ﴿And those who declare their wives unlawful by zihar and then retract what they said — the freeing of a slave before they touch each other. That is what you are admonished with. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ ﴿But whoever does not find [a slave], then fasting two consecutive months before they touch each other. But whoever is unable, then feeding sixty needy people. That is so that you may believe in Allah and His Messenger. These are the limits of Allah. And for the disbelievers is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who oppose Allah and His Messenger will be humiliated as those before them were humiliated. And We have already sent down clear signs, and for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment.﴾ ﴿On the Day when Allah will resurrect them all and inform them of what they did. Allah has enumerated it, and they have forgotten it. And Allah is Witness over all things.﴾ ﴿Have you not considered that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth? There is no private conversation of three but that He is their fourth, nor of five but that He is their sixth, nor of less than that or more but that He is with them wherever they are. Then He will inform them of what they did on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾
